<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Consider the one-sided binomial confidence interval
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_001">
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                          <m:mfenced close=")" open="(">
                            <m:mrow>
                              <m:mi>L</m:mi>
                              <m:mo>,</m:mo>
                              <m:mn>1</m:mn>
                            </m:mrow>
                          </m:mfenced>
                        </m:math>
                        <jats:tex-math>$\left(L,1\right)$</jats:tex-math>
                        <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_001.png"/>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    containing the unknown parameter
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    when all
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    trials are successful, and the significance level
                    <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                    to be five or one percent. We develop two functions (one for each level) that represent approximations within
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_002">
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                          <m:mi>α</m:mi>
                          <m:mo>/</m:mo>
                          <m:msqrt>
                            <m:mrow>
                              <m:mn>3</m:mn>
                            </m:mrow>
                          </m:msqrt>
                        </m:math>
                        <jats:tex-math>$\alpha /\sqrt{3}$</jats:tex-math>
                        <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_002.png"/>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    of the exact lower-bound
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    =
                    <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      1/
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    . Both the exponential (referred to as a modified rule of three) and the logarithmic function are shown to outperform the standard rule of three
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    ≃ 1 − 3/
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    over each of their respective ranges, that together encompass all sample sizes
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    ≥ 1. Specifically for the exponential, we find that
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_003">
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                          <m:mi>exp</m:mi>
                          <m:mfenced close=")" open="(">
                            <m:mrow>
                              <m:mo>−</m:mo>
                              <m:mn>3</m:mn>
                              <m:mo>/</m:mo>
                              <m:mi>n</m:mi>
                            </m:mrow>
                          </m:mfenced>
                        </m:math>
                        <jats:tex-math>$\mathrm{exp}\left(-3/n\right)$</jats:tex-math>
                        <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_003.png"/>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    is a better lower bound when
                    <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                    = 0.05 and
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    < 1054 and that
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_004">
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                          <m:mi>exp</m:mi>
                          <m:mfenced close=")" open="(">
                            <m:mrow>
                              <m:mo>−</m:mo>
                              <m:mn>4.6569</m:mn>
                              <m:mo>/</m:mo>
                              <m:mi>n</m:mi>
                            </m:mrow>
                          </m:mfenced>
                        </m:math>
                        <jats:tex-math>$\mathrm{exp}\left(-4.6569/n\right)$</jats:tex-math>
                        <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/j_ijb-2022-0061_ineq_004.png"/>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    is a better bound when
                    <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                    = 0.01 and
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    < 209.
                  </jats:p>
title: A modified rule of three for the one-sided binomial confidence interval
